transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

I’m here because I just can’t seem to keep my work in order anymore. At the laundry, I’ve got tickets, receipts, notes, customer jobs… they all end up piled together, and then I don’t know what I’m supposed to handle first. It’s been getting really frustrating.
When did you first start noticing these problems with keeping things organized and prioritized—did this begin recently, or has it been a pattern since you were a child?

It’s been a pattern for a long time, honestly. Even back in grade school, teachers would tell my mom I was bright, but kind of scattered. I’d talk out of turn, lose papers, and I needed reminders to actually finish my work. So it’s not really new—it’s just harder to manage now.
Besides feeling disorganized, do you often feel restless, fidgety, or like you need to be constantly moving or talking, even when you're supposed to be sitting still?

Yes, I do. Like at church committee meetings, or those fabric-care trainings for work, I have a hard time just staying seated. I’ll keep finding reasons to get up—get water, grab papers, check on something—even when everyone else is sitting still. It’s like I feel better if I’m moving.
Do you often find yourself interrupting conversations, blurting out answers before someone finishes a question, or having trouble waiting your turn in line or in discussions?

Yes, I do. At work I’ll cut into my staff’s conversations, or I’ll reach over and fix how they’re sorting clothes before they even ask me. I don’t always mean to, but I know it can come off like I’m butting in.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient demonstrates chronic, childhood-onset symptoms of both inattention (disorganization, losing papers, difficulty prioritizing, needing reminders to finish tasks) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, excessive movement, interrupting others, intruding on others' activities). Symptoms have persisted since grade school and currently cause functional impairment across multiple settings (work, community/church activities), meeting criteria for combined presentation ADHD (F90.2) rather than a predominantly inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive subtype.
